qs.q: A patient with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia develops symptoms of warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. Which confirmatory test is used to detect the presence of antibodies or complement on the surface of the red blood cells?
o: C. Bone marrow trephine biopsy procedure
qs.e: The direct antiglobulin Coombs test directly detects antibodies or complement bound to the red blood cell surface in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. The indirect test detects antibodies circulating in the serum.
qs.s: Acute Leukaemia (AML/ALL) & WBC Disorders: Haematology Guide: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with suspected chronic lymphocytic leukaemia presents with headache and blurred vision. What is the investigation of choice to assess for malignant cell infiltration of the central nervous system?
o: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
Serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains
qs.e: Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid cytology allows direct assessment for malignant cell infiltration in central nervous system involvement. Imaging modalities like MRI do not provide definitive cellular confirmation of malignant infiltration.
qs.s: Acute Leukaemia (AML/ALL) & WBC Disorders: Haematology Guide: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following interventions or tests confirms warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia as a complication in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia?
qs.e: The direct antiglobulin Coombs test confirms autoimmune haemolytic anaemia by detecting antibodies or complement proteins on the red blood cell surface. The indirect test detects antibodies in serum and is used for pre-transfusion testing.
qs.s: Acute Leukaemia (AML/ALL) & WBC Disorders: Haematology Guide: MCQs

qs.q: Which specific cell type or abnormality on a peripheral blood smear is the hallmark of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia?
qs.e: Smudge cells, resulting from the rupture of fragile neoplastic lymphocytes during slide preparation, are characteristic of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. Auer rods are diagnostic features of acute myeloid leukaemia.
qs.s: Pathology Practical and Stains Revision Guide: MCQs

qs.q: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is characterized by accumulation of
o: Accumulation of mature monoclonal B lymphocytes
qs.e: CLL is a clonal proliferation of functionally incompetent mature B cells (CD5+, CD23+, CD19+) that accumulate in blood, marrow, and lymph nodes.

ai.clinicalScope: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) in adult patients presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
ai.title: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: CLL is a clonal proliferation of CD5⁺ B‑cells causing progressive lymphocytosis, lymphadenopathy and immunodeficiency. Diagnosis relies on peripheral blood morphology and immunophenotype; staging guides treatment in settings where targeted therapy is limited.

sections.p: CLL is a mature B‑cell neoplasm characterised by ≥5 × 10⁹/L clonal lymphocytes in peripheral blood, smudge cells on smear, and a CD5⁺ CD20⁺ immunophenotype.
b: Peripheral smear: abundant small mature lymphocytes with smudge cells
Flow cytometry: CD5⁺ CD19⁺ CD20⁺ CD23⁺ surface Ig low
Bone‑marrow biopsy (if available): interstitial infiltration by small lymphocytes

sections.p: The Rai and Binet systems are used; they rely on clinical findings rather than expensive labs, making them suitable for low‑resource settings.
b: Rai stage 0–IV based on lymphocytosis, adenopathy, organomegaly, anaemia, thrombocytopenia
Binet A‑C based on number of lymphoid areas involved and cytopenias

sections.p: CLL is usually sporadic; however, certain infections and environmental factors increase risk in East Africa.
b: Age >60 years (most common risk factor)
Chronic immune stimulation (e.g., HIV, malaria) – modest association
Exposure to agricultural pesticides – reported in rural cohorts
Family history of lymphoid malignancy

sections.p: Patients often present with painless lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and fatigue from anaemia or infections.
b: Generalised or cervical/axillary lymphadenopathy
Splenomegaly causing early satiety
Recurrent bacterial infections due to hypogammaglobulinaemia
Incidental lymphocytosis on routine CBC

sections.p: Prioritise tests that answer specific clinical questions; when a test is unavailable, use the next best alternative.

t.b: Is there lymphocytosis and cytopenia? – Lymphocyte count ≥5 × 10⁹/L confirms suspicion; anaemia/thrombocytopenia upstage disease
Are smudge cells present? – Numerous smudge cells support CLL; absence prompts search for other leukaemias
Does the immunophenotype match CLL? – CD5⁺ CD19⁺ CD20⁺ CD23⁺ confirms diagnosis; lack of CD5 suggests other B‑cell disorders
Is hypogammaglobulinaemia present? – Low IgG explains infection risk; guides need for IVIG
Is splenomegaly present? – Palpable spleen >2 cm below costal margin indicates advanced stage

b: Rapidly rising lymphocyte count (>50 % in 1 month) – suggests transformation (Richter’s)
Severe anaemia (Hb <8 g/dL) or thrombocytopenia (<30 × 10⁹/L) – risk of bleeding or cardiac strain
Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia or immune thrombocytopenia – requires immunosuppression
Infections with opportunistic organisms (e.g., Pneumocystis) – treat promptly

sections.p: Therapy is guided by stage, symptoms and resource availability; watch‑and‑wait is appropriate for early disease.
b: Watch‑and‑wait for Rai 0‑I or Binet A without symptoms
Chemoimmunotherapy (e.g., chlorambucil + anti‑CD20 monoclonal antibody) when disease progresses – chosen for oral administration and tolerability
Avoid fludarabine in HIV‑positive patients due to profound immunosuppression
Supportive care: prophylactic antibiotics, immunoglobulin replacement for recurrent infections, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal) before therapy

sections.p: Regular monitoring detects progression and treatment toxicity.
b: CBC every 3 months for stage 0‑I, every 1–2 months after therapy initiation
Physical exam for new lymphadenopathy or organomegaly each visit
Educate patients on infection signs and prompt reporting
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and HPV where feasible to reduce secondary malignancy risk

sections.p: Several haematologic and solid‑tumour conditions mimic CLL.
b: Waldenström macroglobulinaemia – IgM paraprotein, hyperviscosity, no CD5 expression
Hairy cell leukaemia – TRAP‑positive cells, splenomegaly with dry tap, CD25⁺ CD103⁺
Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – blasts on smear, TdT⁺, rapid progression

sections.p: Interpretation pitfalls common in low‑resource labs.
b: Smudge cells may be over‑reported in poorly prepared slides – correlate with absolute lymphocyte count
Flow cytometry gating errors can miss low‑level CD5 expression – repeat if clinical suspicion high
Serum Ig levels can be normal early in disease – repeat if infections recur

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of fever with neutropenia
Severe dyspnoea or chest pain suggesting pulmonary embolism or infection
Unexplained bruising or bleeding with platelets <30 × 10⁹/L
Rapidly enlarging lymph nodes causing airway compromise

faq.q: Why is watch‑and‑wait safe in early CLL?
faq.a: Early disease is indolent; treatment does not improve survival and adds toxicity, so observation avoids unnecessary side effects.

faq.q: What is the significance of smudge cells?
faq.a: They are fragile lymphocytes that rupture during slide preparation; abundant smudge cells are a classic clue to CLL.

faq.q: How does HIV affect CLL management?
faq.a: HIV‑related immunosuppression increases infection risk; fludarabine is avoided and regimens with lower myelosuppression are preferred.

exam: A 68‑year‑old farmer presents with painless cervical nodes and a lymphocyte count of 7 × 10⁹/L. What is your next diagnostic step? — Order a peripheral smear and flow cytometry to confirm CLL immunophenotype.
Why would you choose chlorambucil over fludarabine in this patient? — Chlorambucil is oral, less myelosuppressive, and safer in settings with limited infection control.
A patient on watch‑and‑wait develops new anaemia (Hb 7 g/dL). How does this change management? — Progresses to treatment indication; start chemoimmunotherapy and evaluate for autoimmune haemolysis.
What clinical feature distinguishes CLL from Waldenström macroglobulinaemia? — Presence of IgM paraprotein and hyperviscosity symptoms in Waldenström, absent in CLL.
How would you monitor for Richter’s transformation in a low‑resource hospital? — Look for rapid lymph node growth, B symptoms, and rising LDH; confirm with tissue biopsy if feasible.
A patient with CLL develops recurrent sinopulmonary infections. What supportive measure is indicated? — Provide immunoglobulin replacement therapy and vaccinate against encapsulated organisms.
Explain why a high lymphocyte count alone does not always mean treatment is required. — Treatment is based on symptoms, cytopenias, and organ involvement, not just count.
What red‑flag laboratory result would prompt urgent referral? — Platelet count <30 × 10⁹/L or haemoglobin <8 g/dL indicating severe cytopenia.
